vignette:
He is 35, a South Eastern Asian man who now works as an accountant in a midsize logistics company, and when he begins telling his story, he does so the way he handles spreadsheets—carefully, line by line, as if precision might keep the worst parts contained.

Before the trauma, he describes himself as organized, quiet, and dependable. He had been married then, newly settled into adult life, working long hours but taking pride in being the person in the office who caught mistakes others missed. He says he liked numbers because they behaved predictably. Then, during a period of political unrest in his home country, he was detained. He does not initially use the word torture. He says only that he was taken, held in a place with no windows, and made to understand very quickly that time, sleep, and pain no longer belonged to him.

Over several conversations, more of it emerges. He is beaten repeatedly. He is tied in stress positions until his muscles spasm and his shoulders feel as if they are being pulled apart. He is doused with cold water and questioned for hours, sometimes days, about things he insists he does not know. He learns the sound of boots in the corridor, the scrape of a metal chair, the particular silence that comes just before someone enters. He comes to fear not only the pain but the waiting. The uncertainty is almost worse. He remembers trying to survive by shrinking inward, focusing on tiny calculations: how many breaths he can count before the door opens, how long he can stare at a crack in the wall without blinking, whether he can make himself feel less human and therefore less vulnerable.

After his release, he returns home physically thinner and emotionally unrecognizable to himself. He tells almost no one what happened. His former wife knows enough to see that something is wrong, but he cannot bear her questions or her touch. At night he jerks awake drenched in sweat, certain for a few seconds that he is back in the cell. Sometimes he wakes already on his feet. He starts checking the locks repeatedly before bed, then checking them again. If a motorcycle backfires outside or someone knocks unexpectedly at the door, his whole body reacts before his mind catches up. He drops into a crouch once in his own kitchen, ashamed even as it is happening.

When he eventually emigrates and rebuilds his life elsewhere, he chooses accounting in part because it offers structure, a world governed by rules and reconciliation. His colleagues know him as meticulous and somewhat distant. They appreciate that he is never late, that his reports are exact, that he notices discrepancies no one else sees. What they do not see is how much effort it takes for him to sit with his back to the open office. He scans reflections in computer monitors to track movement behind him. When a senior manager raises his voice during a meeting, even in ordinary frustration, he stops hearing the words and feels instead a rush of heat, then cold, then a blankness that leaves him nodding without understanding.

He avoids crowded elevators and windowless conference rooms. He keeps explanations ready—too much coffee, poor sleep, a headache. He takes the stairs even to the twelfth floor. On certain days, especially when he is exhausted, the fluorescent buzz in the office and the hum of the air-conditioning blend into something that reminds him of the detention room, and his chest tightens so abruptly he has to go lock himself in a restroom stall until the feeling passes. He presses his palms against his thighs and tells himself where he is: tax quarter, Thursday, office building, safe. Sometimes it works quickly. Sometimes not.

His marriage does not survive the years after the trauma. He says his ex-wife wanted him present, and he was physically there but rarely reachable. He could not explain why he recoiled when she touched his shoulders from behind, or why he spent whole evenings silent, staring at the television without following the plot. Arguments became easier than intimacy. Even now, divorced and living alone, he keeps his apartment sparse. He likes to be able to see everything at once. He chooses a corner table in restaurants, if he goes at all, and mentally maps exits on arrival.

He is tired of being governed by fear and just as tired of pretending he is not afraid. What troubles him most is not only the memories themselves but how alive they remain. He does not remember the detention as something finished and filed away in the past. It intrudes into ordinary moments—the slam of a door, the smell of damp concrete, the sight of restraints in a medical setting—and suddenly his body is convinced the danger is current. He knows, rationally, that he is a 35-year-old accountant in a different country, divorced, employed, paying rent, answering emails. Yet part of him still lives in that room with no windows, listening for footsteps, bracing for the door.
